entries.title: As Affordability Concerns Persist, Could D.C. Reduce Parking and Traffic Fines?
entries.summary: Lawmakers have discussed the possibility, but making tickets cheaper could be costly for D.C.
entries.content:
Few people agree on most things, but D.C. residents and visitors alike often find common ground on one gripe: Parking and traffic tickets are plentiful and expensive.

But new proposals in the Wilson Building are reviving discussions around whether D.C. should reduce the fines associated with parking and traffic tickets, with some lawmakers contemplating fully cutting them in half while others propose doing away with the practice of doubling fines after 30 days.

“I do think we need to address this problem,” D.C. Council Chair Phil Mendelson said this week. “We are seeing tickets issued in much greater volume. In a sense that’s a good thing because there are bad drivers. However it means that fines are racked up quickly and are quite hefty. There are drivers that owe thousands of dollars. That’s not sustainable.”

Earlier this month, At-Large council member Robert White proposed halving all parking fines, which start as low as $20 for parking within five feet of an alley and can increase quickly thereafter: Parking in a restricted rush hour zone can fetch a $100 ticket, blocking an emergency snow route is $250 and excessive idling is $500.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

“Residents are drowning in costs,” White said. “[They] have to stretch every single paycheck further just to cover the basics. I’m hearing about this every day in every part of the city. A parking ticket can make the difference between covering bills and falling behind, but it is not just those making minimum wage who are feeling the squeeze and stressed by it right now.”

In the 2025 fiscal year, D.C. issued 1,093,880 parking tickets worth more than $59 million in fines. White said the average parking ticket fine that year was $59.20, which at the city’s current minimum wage would take more than three hours of work for some residents to pay off.

This week Ward 8 council member Trayon White — who has long argued that D.C.’s parking and traffic fines are too high — introduced a bill that would end the existing doubling of any fine if it’s not paid within 30 days of the ticket being issued.

“I believe that drivers should slow down and drive safely. We can hold motorists accountable without financially devastating them,” he said on Tuesday. “If I don’t have the money in 10 days I don’t have double the money after 30 days.”

Mendelson — who himself said he would favor cutting parking fines in half — said his colleagues should also look at the cost of tickets issued by the city’s many traffic cameras; those fines start at $100 and escalate rapidly, especially as a driver’s speeding gets more egregious. (In 2025 D.C.’s traffic cameras issued 3.3 million tickets.)

Still, the populist impulse to respond to D.C. residents’ affordability concerns would be costly, and past efforts to reduce fines have fallen short because of the fiscal reality that any reductions in revenue from the fines would lead to reduced spending on other programs and services.

“I’d love to see how we could reduce those things,” said Ward 6 council member Charles Allen, the chair of the council’s transportation committee. “The reality is, unless I have something to offset it — especially in lean budget years when we’re scrambling to help protect funding for child care and health care and housing — it makes it increasingly hard.”

The reason D.C. is virtually dependent on revenue from parking and traffic tickets has to do with the city budget. Every year the mayor and council craft a budget not just for the upcoming fiscal year but also the three that follow. Those budgets — which by law have to be balanced — are built on estimates of how much revenue the city is taking in, from traditional sources like taxes and fees but also parking and traffic tickets.

In 2025 the value of all fines from parking, traffic cameras and moving offenses amounted to more than $754 million, out of an annual budget hovering in the $11 billion range. That year, some $316 million worth of fines were actually paid. Reducing those fines would mean replacing the revenue the associated tickets were supposed to bring over four years.

“It's hard to justify cutting tickets in half when we’re cutting education programs and food assistance,” said Ward 5 council member Zachary Parker earlier this month.

This is not a new political and fiscal reality for many council members. In 2018 the council actually passed a bill authored by Trayon White that would have changed the point at which an unpaid fine doubles, from 30 days to 60. It was never implemented, though, because it would have cost $111 million in revenue over four years.

Robert White’s idea of halving parking fines was estimated to cost D.C. between $10 and $20 million in revenue annually.

Lawmakers have tried to break the costly link between fines and the city’s broader budget. Within the past five years, the council mandated that fines from traffic cameras be invested only in traffic safety programs, but Mayor Muriel Bowser redirected the funds back into the general budget, where they have remained since.

Whether D.C.’s likely next mayor will do anything differently remains to be seen. Asked by The Washington Sun whether reducing parking and traffic fines would be on her radar, Ward 4 Council member Janeese Lewis George said there were more elements to consider than a ticket left on a windshield or mailed to a driver.

“We have to balance affordability and the conversation around enforcement and accountability,” she said. “We’ve also had a number of traffic crashes. We've lost lives. A number of times when we look up the tickets of the person who committed some of those dangerous behaviors they have a large amount of tickets. It’s a nuanced conversation.”

And one that she’s been hearing more and more about. “It’s the one thing people yell at me, they’ll say, ‘My tickets are too high!’” she added.

There have been other attempts to address the issue. Earlier this year D.C. implemented a pilot program where it gave a one-time 50% discount on minor traffic tickets to residents receiving food benefits, based on research showing that income-based fines can sometimes increase payment rates while promoting safer driving. A traffic safety bill authored by Allen and passed by the council in late 2024 would give residents a chance to take driver safety classes in lieu of paying $500 in traffic fines, but the program hasn’t been funded.

Trayon White has also introduced separate bills to address D.C.’s parking and traffic fines. One would expand the use of traffic amnesties, where the city waives fees and interest on unpaid fines during designated periods. Bowser ran a four-month amnesty in 2021, when more than 32,000 drivers settled tickets worth some $44 million in fines. Another of his bills would allow drivers to do community service in lieu of any fines they owe.

entries.title: Monica De La Cruz’s Reelection Bid Is Testing Trump’s Fragile Coalition in South Texas
entries.summary: The Republican is fighting to keep a coalition of Latino voters together as she runs against a ubiquitous opponent, Tejano star Bobby Pulido.
entries.content:
EDINBURG, Texas — Election Day was only 14 days away, but Rep. Monica De La Cruz wasn’t, technically, campaigning. She was touring affordable housing in her district alongside a Cabinet secretary instead.

The Republican is up for reelection against Tejano music star Bobby Pulido in a majority-Latino district where President Donald Trump made stunning gains the last time he ran. How De La Cruz navigates the next stretch could determine how both parties approach Latino voters nationally in the coming years.

She faces significant headwinds.

Voters who backed her in the past aren’t particularly loyal to either party and are frustrated by what they see as inaction and Trump’s lack of success, after voting for him enthusiastically just two years ago. Trump’s popularity with Latino voters has deteriorated, according to a Pew Research Center poll released earlier this month, which found his approval rating with the group down from 38% in February 2025 to 24% among those surveyed.

De La Cruz, however, demurred when asked if she was worried about losing the inroads Republicans have made with Latino voters in South Texas.

“This is one of the most competitive races across the nation, and what I've decided to do is to focus on my race and what I'm able to bring to the table,” she told The Washington Sun.

De La Cruz isn’t only fighting against a tough national environment for Republicans. Pulido has proven himself to be a formidable opponent running on his celebrity, with an uncanny ability to generate national headlines.

“The [Rio Grande Valley] is the bellwether, so what happens in Texas-15, what happens in the RGV, will set the narrative for investment in Latino voters in the future,” said Melissa Morales, the president of the Somos PAC, a Democratic-aligned group that invests in increasing Latino voter turnout across the country.

Is the Republican Party’s breakthrough with Latino voters a fragile coalition built around Trump’s promises of bringing prices down and improving the economy, or something more permanent?

De La Cruz’s approach suggests she’s not banking on the latter: Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner’s visit to South Texas this week to help highlight De La Cruz's work on affordable housing gave the Republican incumbent a chance to spotlight her record.

The event also put her front and center on an issue that resonates with Latino voters: housing affordability, a major concern according to a Pew study.

“I am so proud to have the secretary here because what it shows is our commitment to affordable housing and families, right here in the Rio Grande Valley, being able to achieve their American dream, which is owning their first home,” De La Cruz told reporters after the tour of homes.

The district has since been redrawn in an effort to help Republicans pick up seats, but in 2024, Trump carried Texas' 15th Congressional District by nearly 18 percentage points, while De La Cruz won a second term in Congress. For how much the president is hanging over the race, De La Cruz was studious about not bringing him up.

She did not mention Trump during her official office stops on Tuesday and has pitched herself to voters as someone who would fight against his administration’s immigration policy.

She put out an ad last month featuring the story of a DACA recipient who was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The ad suggested that De La Cruz helped release the man from detention.

“I have been direct with leadership from Day 1,” she told The Sun. “I have told leadership that enforcement must focus on the cartels and the criminals, not hardworking families that are trying to navigate the very complex immigration system that we have.”

She’s not only focused on policy issues. She has also made a case against Pulido by accusing him of protecting a former bandmate, Frankie Caballero, a registered sex offender who was convicted of indecent sexual contact with a child. Pulido has repeatedly denied knowing about the conviction.

Pulido, in turn, has accused De La Cruz of bending to the Trump administration and not fighting for South Texans. He has framed the administration as being too tough on migrants and responsible for the increased cost of living.

But he’s also holding the Democratic Party at arm’s length, pitching himself as someone who would fight for South Texans over the party.

“We don't care about parties down here. We don't,” Pulido told The Sun in an interview before a concert-turned-campaign rally on Saturday. “People care more about the candidate than they do about a party platform, and I think that's where the rest of the country is. That's kind of where we've always been.”

The arena for his farewell concert on Saturday was packed: Thousands of fans in cowboy boots and hats streamed into Bert Ogden Arena in Edinburg, holding micheladas, margaritas, nachos dripping with melted cheese and boxes of popcorn.

They came to hear Pulido perform his signature hit, “Desvelado,” one last time, but also for his pitch on why he should be the next representative of Texas’s 15th Congressional District.

He focused on affordability, like many other Democrats on the trail this fall. Pulido, an Edinburg native, also pointed to his roots in South Texas, mentioning an uncle who was a former county judge and another who was a former prosecutor, for why he should be elected to office.

One voter who attended, Orly Rodriguez, said he plans to vote for Pulido because of his campaign promises.

“To me, it's not about, you know, Democrat, Republican,” Rodriguez told the Sun. “To me, it's about the individual, and I'm focusing on him personally.”

entries.title: State Asked Foreign Service Officers Up for Promotion Whether They Voted for Trump
entries.summary: Federal law strictly prohibits making civil service personnel decisions on the basis of political affiliation.
entries.content:
The State Department has asked some foreign service officials up for promotion who they voted for in the 2016, 2020 and 2024 presidential elections, raising concerns the agency is violating a federal law that bars politicized personnel decisions within the nonpartisan ranks.

Top officials in the State Department made clear that only candidates who voted for President Donald Trump would be eligible for the mid-to-upper level foreign service roles. They also told candidates that their campaign donation history would be examined and any donation to Democrats would be disqualifying.

The Washington Sun spoke to six current and former State Department officials familiar with the line of questioning around candidates’ voting histories. Three of the sources had spoken directly with individuals who had been asked the questions.

Congressional Democrats have been preparing to probe such incidents.

“The Committee has been following allegations that the Trump Administration is making political affiliation a factor in employment for some time now,” Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, told The Washington Sun in a statement. “These are critical national security positions and individuals should be chosen for their experience and ability, not their political loyalty. We are working with the House and other relevant committees to thoroughly investigate all such claims.”

While the federal government employs thousands of political appointees who turnover with each administration, the vast majority of the government workforce are permanent, career staff intended to be shielded from political interference.

Federal law directly prohibits federal officials from making any personnel decisions on the basis of political affiliation.

A spokesperson for the State Department declined to comment on the voting history questions but emphasized the importance of “fidelity” in a statement.

“Fidelity means upholding the Constitution and the law and executing policy with loyalty to the American people and their interests,” the spokesperson said. “It emphasizes the critical importance of service, integrity, and policy alignment across the Foreign Service. It is not about partisan behavior but rather about executing the president’s vision for foreign policy.”

The spokesperson added that Secretary Marco Rubio has prioritized merit and rewarding “demonstrated performance on behalf of administration priorities” in promoting career staff into leadership positions.

In July of last year, the State Department added a “fidelity” section to the foreign service’s performance-evaluation process, requiring managers to assess employees’ commitment to “completely aligning oneself and one’s team to the most current [U.S. government] goals.”

The department also announced last year it was remaking the Foreign Service Officer Test, which all candidates must pass. One person who recently took the exam said it included questions about the impact of former President Ronald Reagan’s tax policies and the accomplishments of Trump’s Mike Pompeo, who was secretary of State during Trump’s first term.

“There was just something about the test that made it seem like they weren’t looking for the highest scores but people who answered a certain way on specific questions,” the person said.

Trump and Rubio have moved to remake the nation’s diplomatic corps. The State Department has shed nearly one-fourth of its workforce through layoffs and various separation incentives. It has awarded a $1 million, no-bid contract to a recruitment firm whose CEO has said more Christians should serve in government and hiring at the department had become too “woke.”

As The Washington Sun reported, veteran foreign service officials have also been boxed out of senior positions, asked to resign and sidelined in major foreign policy decisions. Those efforts have led to a wave of recent departures from the diplomatic corps’ top ranks.

“This is more evidence that there is conduct to get rid of folks because of perceived political affiliations,” one congressional aide not authorized to speak to the press said of the State Department asking foreign service candidates about their voting history.

The Trump administration has faced some legal action against its efforts to identify supporters among the civil service.

It previously overhauled the federal hiring process by requiring applicants to write short essays on their favorite Trump policies, but it subsequently replaced those questions under court order.

Federal workers’ unions have also sued over the administration’s plans to create a new class of workers who can be fired for any reason.

Max Stier, president of the Partnership for Public Service, a good government advocacy group, said State’s latest actions mark an “appalling and flagrant disregard of federal law” designed to protect federal workers from being evaluated based on political allegiance.

“This is yet another shocking example of the Trump administration hurtling our government back in time to the spoils system of the 19th century,” Stier said. “Ultimately, it’s the safety and security of the American people that are being compromised.”

entries.title: Abdul El-Sayed Wants MAHA Voters
entries.summary: Some of the Michigan Democrat’s proposals align with RFK Jr.’s MAHA movement. But El-Sayed’s nonnegotiables complicate his pitch.
entries.content:
MUSKEGON, Mich. — John Trocke is at a place he’s never been before: considering whether to vote for a Democrat. Specifically, Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.

The 42-year-old architect from Holland, Michigan, has been frustrated with the Trump administration’s failure to adopt the majority of Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Make America Healthy Again platform.

“Republicans need to be spanked a bit in this coming midterm,” Trocke said. “I've become so disenchanted with the GOP that I've opened myself … to different possibilities.”

Trocke is one of a growing cadre of MAHA voters around the nation who say the Trump administration has failed to make good on the promises of the 2024 presidential race. He’s also part of a voting bloc that El-Sayed believes he can lure away from Republicans.

El-Sayed’s platform, which includes several policies aligned closely with MAHA priorities on food quality, pesticides and breaking apart monopolies in America’s food system, has interested Trocke, who already supported El-Sayed’s views on Iran and Israel.

“I think [RFK Jr.] has sold out his movement,” El-Sayed said in an interview with The Washington Sun on Monday. The former Wayne County health director added that he worked on and wrote about these issues before Robert F. Kennedy Jr. ran for president.

“I want to be talking about what we can actually do to take that mantle, [and] stand up against corporations,” El-Sayed said.

MAHA supporters never cleanly fit in either party. Kennedy, who himself was a longtime Democrat before 2023, helped Republicans expand their tent to include voters motivated by environmental and wellness causes, including anti-vaccine activists.

But the MAHA movement has been hot and cold on Republicans’ record. The administration began to phase out synthetic red food coloring and scaled back childhood vaccines, but the MAHA movement is still frustrated that President Donald Trump and Kennedy haven’t done more to go after food conglomerates and were deeply critical of Trump’s decision to loosen regulations on pesticides and other chemicals.

Whether that anger gives candidates like El-Sayed a shot at more votes depends on what these MAHA voters want to prioritize — and whether they’re willing to fully turn against Kennedy.

“RFK Jr. is kind of one of our iconic leaders,” said Rachel Atwood, an organizer in Western Michigan’s MAHA community who likes El-Sayed’s position on banning pesticides, but says she’s still likely to vote for Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers. “Can [El-Sayed] win over MAHA voters based on dyes and pesticides when he has now … verbalized support of vaccine [mandates] and has attacked RFK Jr. for questioning them?”

El-Sayed has nonnegotiables. He’s adamant about vaccines and is a sharp critic of Kennedy’s. He accused the health secretary of being “bought by corporations” in his interview with The Sun, and promised to open an investigation into how the Department of Health and Human Services handled the recent cyclospora outbreak if appointed to the Senate committee overseeing HHS.

“Eight thousand Michiganders were infected, and possibly, probably many, many more,” El-Sayed said of the outbreak. “I really want to subpoena him and understand why this happened.”

El-Sayed’s position on vaccines was a deal-breaker for Atwood.

For Trocke, who is vaccinated and aligns more with the anti-pesticide side of RFK’s platform, El-Sayed could do more to soften his approach toward Kennedy.

“If he were to even express some magnanimous attitude towards RFK himself,” Trocke said, “I think that would be a positive thing, and would certainly be appealing to those of us who were in that RFK camp.”

El-Sayed told The Sun he is willing to work with the health secretary — between the subpoenas.

“Where we can work together to serve Michiganders, we will, and where I need to hold him accountable to serve Michiganders, I will,” he said.

If he makes it to Washington in January, El-Sayed said he would also reach out to HHS to probe Kennedy’s leadership.

“I know for sure that there are a lot of people who work underneath [RFK Jr.] who are so disaffected by him and his leadership style,” El-Sayed said. “I will be having those conversations.”

El-Sayed says the strongest policy overlaps between his health platform and the existing MAHA movement center on processed foods and monopolies. Monopolies in America’s food system would be his first point of attack if elected to the Senate.

But while health is a regular focus of El-Sayed’s campaign stops — his calls for single-payer Medicare received some of the loudest cheers of the night at a recent town hall in Muskegon — the Democrat’s stump speech doesn’t always champion the more MAHA-coded policies in his platform.

Tasha Schurgin, a longtime organizer with Michigan for Vaccine Choice, believes El-Sayed is simply throwing the MAHA community crumbs to gain their vote.

“If you're going to say, ‘Hey, I support the MAHA movement,’ you've got to really support it wholeheartedly. You can't pick and choose what you want to support,” said Schurgin, who lives in the greater Detroit area and considers vaccines her top issue. She is voting for Rogers, who she calls the lesser of two evils.

“By no means do I think Mike Rogers is a champion of the MAHA movement or vaccine choice,” she said. “But I don't also see him trying to capitalize on it and be a wolf in sheep's clothing.”

The Rogers campaign did not return a request for comment.

Atwood points out, however, that factions of the MAHA movement still have the potential to be swayed by El-Sayed’s policies.

Trocke falls into that category. He voted for Trump in 2016 but left the presidential race blank on his ballot in the last two elections. RFK’s support for Trump in 2024 nearly lured him back to vote for the president, but this year, he has already decided he will not vote for Mike Rogers.

He’s still undecided, though, on whether he will vote for El-Sayed or leave that part of the ballot blank.

“Policy statements are easy to print and produce,” Trocke said. “But I think it certainly appears to be a good step that he came out with something.”

entries.title: The Capitals Sure Have Missed Pierre-Luc Dubois
entries.summary: After being sidelined with illness for the last five games, the center is close to a return.
entries.content:
The last week has seen the full range of these Capitals. Here is a team capable of fluid, seamless hockey, as it showed against the Devils and Canadiens, and here is a team capable of the complete opposite, as it showed in a fumbling loss to the Kings. And in both situations, as well as in every intermediate variation, here is a team who could be much improved by the presence of Pierre-Luc Dubois.

Washington may soon be in luck there. Dubois rejoined his teammates in a regular jersey for the duration of practice on Wednesday.

It was his first time doing so in nearly two weeks. The veteran center has missed the last five games with an unspecified illness and was able to return to the facility only in the last few days in a non-contact jersey. He remains on injured reserve. But his appearance at practice on Wednesday bodes well for a potential return in the Capitals’ next game on Saturday. (As does the fact that the team has already sent forward Jonny Brodzinski back down to AHL Hershey.) His recent absence has only underscored his value.

“When he’s healthy, he’s one of the best 200-foot centermen in the game,” said Capitals forward Tom Wilson. “I love playing with him.”

That 200-foot skillset has been sorely missed. Dubois is an essential component of this offense and part of the first unit on the power play. He’s also the best defensive center on this roster. For a team still grasping at consistency, with a number of young players and new pieces, Dubois can offer a critical steadying force.

“Obviously, a huge piece of the team,” Washington forward Boone Jenner said of Dubois after the first game without him. “When you lose him, you're losing a big presence up the middle that plays in every situation for us.”

Dubois had three points in the four games that he played before his illness. He’d entered training camp poised for a bounceback year after missing the majority of last season with injuries.

“This year, he came in, he was one of the best conditioned guys on the team,” said Wilson, a linemate of Dubois’. “I know he’s hungry. He wants to make some noise this year.”

Their line had been an early bright spot for the Capitals. With big offseason acquisition Alex Tuch flanking Dubois on the left and Wilson on the right, they offered a rare combination of size, dexterity and speed. All three players are 6’4”. Besides their height, they also share a certain versatility and vision, and they found chemistry together quickly. In their four games together, Tuch, Dubois and Wilson ranked higher in expected goals than any other line combination on the Capitals.

“I think we’re all kind of alike,” Tuch said of their line. “It’s nice playing with a lot of space out there. A lot of time and space. No one’s coming to mess with you.”

Dubois may or may not be slotted back in with Tuch and Wilson. Capitals head coach Spencer Carbery has shuffled his lines as the roster has navigated other injuries and illnesses over the last week: Recent games have seen him split up Tuch and Wilson. That may be simply a temporary measure. (Carbery said earlier this week that his staff has been looking at its line combinations one matchup at a time: “We’ve got to just try to find a way to piece it together a little bit and go with the hot hand.”) But regardless of who he plays with upon his return, Dubois should provide a dynamic, meaningful boost.

The Capitals hope that will extend to the power play. It has continued to be a problem for this group: Washington ranks 31st in the NHL for time spent in the offensive zone during the power play. Almost no other team spends this much time getting bogged down on the other end of the ice and struggling with entry passes.

“It’s got to get better,” Carbery said after the loss on Tuesday, which featured an especially frustrating power play in the third period. “We’ll continue to tinker around with personnel, and look at some different things, starting different units. But it has to get better.”

To that end, Washington assistant coach Ray Bennett spent extra time with the power play units at practice on Wednesday. That group could finally include Dubois.
entries.author: Emma Baccellieri

entries.title: Ohio's Republican Governor Says Ramaswamy Should Take Down His Acton Ad
entries.summary: Gov. Mike DeWine said the ad featuring a Democratic candidate's estranged mother was “deeply, deeply troubling.”
entries.content:
By Julie Carr Smyth

COLUMBUS, Ohio — Republican Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine has denounced a controversial ad featuring the estranged mother of Dr. Amy Acton, taking sides with the Democratic candidate for governor and former member of his Cabinet over her Republican rival, Vivek Ramaswamy.

At a gathering with reporters at the Statehouse in Columbus, DeWine called the ad “deeply, deeply troubling.”

“It's wrong to run this ad,” he said. “I would urge Ramaswamy's campaign to take this down.”

DeWine's remarks place him at odds with Ramaswamy, whom he has endorsed. The biotech entrepreneur and 2024 presidential candidate has taken responsibility for the 60-second video, which has drawn bipartisan rebukes, and is spending $4 million to broadcast it online and on TV.

Vice President JD Vance defended an ad Wednesday which spotlights the abuse Acton experienced as a child. During a campaign visit to Ohio, Vance told reporters he was “disgusted” by fellow Republicans who were pushing back against the ad, then later drew cheers at a political rally when he defended Ramaswamy.

Vance said he has watched Democrats “throw every dirty trick in the political book at Vivek,” who he considers a close personal friend -- including calling him a ‘murderer’ — while “the whole time Vivek has stood tall and talked about what he wants to accomplish.”
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Feds Arrest Democrat Who Led Virginia’s Redistricting Push
entries.summary: The case against L. Louise Lucas includes accusations of fraud and racketeering involving a cannabis business she co-owns.
entries.content:
Federal authorities on Thursday charged Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas in a sprawling public corruption case that includes fraud and racketeering accusations involving a cannabis business she co-owns.

Several other members of Lucas’ family have also been arrested as part of the investigation, according to the Virginia Scope. She surrendered to authorities early Thursday morning, according to multiple reports.

Lucas, an 82-year-old Democrat, has served in elected office since the 1980s. She was a prominent figure behind the party’s redistricting efforts in Virginia earlier this year — which was ultimately blocked by the state Supreme Court.

The U.S. Supreme Court later declined to hear the case in an unsigned order, effectively killing the effort.

This is a developing story and will be updated.
entries.author: Michelle Del Rey

entries.title: Rep. Joyce Beatty Is Trying to Reveal Trump’s Kennedy Center Communications
entries.summary: Her attorneys also pointed to a newly disclosed consultant report that they say undercuts the administration’s justification for the shutdown.
entries.content:
Rep. Joyce Beatty is asking a federal judge to force the Trump administration to turn over communications about the president’s management of the Kennedy Center, arguing that executive privilege should not shield his decisions as the institution’s chair because the storied arts institution is not a part of the executive branch.

In a court filing Tuesday, the Ohio Democrat’s attorneys said the administration has improperly withheld information about President Donald Trump’s role in the decision to close the performing arts center for two years. They also pointed to a newly disclosed consultant report that they say undercuts the administration’s justification for the shutdown.

Beatty’s lawyers argued that Trump’s communications with Kennedy Center staff about renovations and the closure fall outside the scope of presidential communications privilege because he was acting as the center’s board chair, not in his capacity as president.

“It would do a terrible disservice to the rule of law—to say nothing of disserving the search for truth in this important litigation about a national memorial to a slain President—to permit Defendants to hide the ball in this way,” Beatty’s lawyers wrote, referencing the administration’s “sweeping claim of executive privilege.”

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Beatty’s filing is the latest development in the lawsuit challenging the Trump administration’s control of the Kennedy Center, including its efforts to rename the institution and close its main building for renovations.

The administration has invoked presidential communications privilege to withhold information sought by Beatty’s legal team. Her attorneys argued Tuesday that the administration has failed to adequately identify the specific communications it seeks to protect or establish that Trump personally invoked the privilege for each of them.

Beatty’s attorneys also argued that the privilege, which protects a president’s confidential deliberations, should not extend to the daily management of a performing arts institution that operates outside the executive branch.

The dispute has taken on new significance following the disclosure of a report prepared by real estate consultant JLL on Aug. 20. Beatty’s attorneys said the report, which was not provided to the Kennedy Center’s board, found that a phased renovation was feasible and appeared to contradict information presented to trustees.

The report was not disclosed to Beatty’s legal team until Oct. 19, after depositions had already taken place, according to the filing.

Beatty’s attorneys also cited a document in which JLL was told by Kennedy Center management that “Q3 2028 reopening is absolute; driven by Presidential mandate.”

The statement, they argued, raises questions about whether the two-year closure timeline was independently determined by the center’s consultants or dictated by Trump before the board considered its options.

The filing said Matt Floca, the Kennedy Center’s executive director, testified that Trump had decided on the two-year closure. Beatty’s attorneys argued that the newly disclosed JLL report was directly responsive to their discovery requests about renovation alternatives, scheduling and costs.

They also questioned why Floca did not disclose the report during his deposition, despite being asked about the consultant’s findings.

The administration has maintained that the board’s decision was supported by expert analysis. But Beatty’s attorneys said the evidence raises questions about whether the consultants’ work was independent or shaped by Trump’s preferred outcome.

Beatty’s attorneys argued that the board could have breached its responsibilities as trustees if it relied on a predetermined recommendation while ignoring evidence supporting alternatives.

The filing also renewed concerns about Trump’s threats to demolish the center if his name is not added to the building. Beatty’s attorneys said they need access to communications about those threats to determine whether the renovation plans could change based on the outcome of the separate dispute over the institution’s renaming.

entries.title: D.C. United Loses to FC Cincinnati, 2-1
entries.summary: The loss drops United to 7-10-13, leaving them in 13th place in the MLS standings.
entries.content:
CINCINNATI — David Douděra scored for the first time in MLS, and Teenage Hadebe recorded his first goal with Cincinnati to help beat D.C. United 2-1 on Wednesday night.

Cincinnati (10-11-9) moved into ninth place in the Eastern Conference standings with hopes of clinching a spot in the playoffs for the fifth season in a row.

D.C. United (7-10-13), which has not qualified for the postseason since 2019, sits in 13th.

Douděra opened the scoring in the 14th minute when a deflected ball fell to his feet at the far post for a one-touch finish. Hadebe put Cincinnati ahead in the 55th on a slide at the back post to finish Evander’s free kick.

United defender Kimito Nono tied it at 1-all in the 38th. João Peglow chipped a pass over the defense that Nono settled with his right foot and calmly sent in a shot with his left.

The game was originally scheduled for Sept. 5 before it was postponed due to pitch conditions and player safety concerns created by heavy rains in the Cincinnati area.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: State Department Recalls Diplomatic Staff in Saudi Arabia
entries.summary: The move follows escalating attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis on Saudi Arabia, a key U.S. ally in the region.
entries.content:
The State Department ordered the departure of some nonessential U.S. diplomatic staff and their family members stationed in Saudi Arabia following escalating attacks from Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebel group.

The paramilitary group has “increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions,” a State Department spokesperson wrote in a statement to The Washington Sun, adding that “the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly, including beyond that immediate area.”

The escalating conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis comes at a time when the U.S. and Israel have drawn up plans for renewed strikes on Iran, The New York Times reported Wednesday. With the midterms weeks away and the ongoing war with Iran driving up global oil prices, President Donald Trump earlier this month committed to pausing U.S. strikes on Iran until after Election Day.

State Department officials also called initial reports of a more sweeping removal order withdrawing personnel from U.S. embassies and missions in several countries across the Middle East “inaccurate.”

“The U.S. Department of State issued an ordered departure for non-emergency U.S. government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia only,” Tommy Pigott, a spokesman for the State Department, wrote Wednesday on X.

After the U.S.-Iran war broke out in February, American officials had ordered similar diplomatic drawbacks as the conflict intensified in the Middle East.

The Houthis control a significant portion of western Yemen, a country that borders Saudi Arabia. The Iran-supported paramilitary group killed dozens in an attack on a Yemeni government security forces training camp earlier this week and launched deadly attacks on an airport and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia — which has continued to intercept ballistic missiles and drones fired by the group.

Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia have escalated in recent months for several reasons. Saudi Arabia formally recognizes and supports Yemen’s internationally recognized government in its fight against the paramilitary group. And as a major non-NATO ally for the U.S., Saudi Arabia serves as a target for the Iran-backed Houthis as Trump’s war against Iran drags on.

The U.S. military has also reportedly begun discreetly drawing back and moving American forces at bases in several countries in the region, including Jordan, Qatar and Kuwait, NBC News reported Wednesday.

“We regularly move U.S. service members and assets to optimize mission readiness” Navy Captain Tim Hawkins, U.S. Central Command Spokesperson, wrote in a statement to The Sun.

“We do not discuss related movements for operational security reasons,” Hawkins said, but emphasized that “U.S. forces remain vigilant and ready to protect American personnel and interests across the region.”
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: Construction on Trump’s Arch Could Begin in Two Weeks
entries.summary: The National Capital Planning Commission will meet Nov. 5 to give final review to Trump’s proposed 250-foot arch.
entries.content:
Construction on President Donald Trump’s triumphal arch could start in two weeks pending final approval from a federal commission stacked with Trump appointees, administration lawyers said in a Wednesday court filing.

The National Capital Planning Commission, a panel in charge of approving projects on federal land in the D.C. area, will meet Nov. 5 to give final review to Trump’s proposed 250-foot arch. Construction could “commence immediately” if the commission approves the plan, the Interior Department authorizes work and the National Park Service publishes notice on the same day, the two-page court filing said.

The arch is slated to be built at Memorial Circle outside of Arlington National Cemetery on an island in the Potomac River. The site sits within the borders of D.C. but is adjacent to Arlington.

Ahead of the November vote, the Trump administration has replaced career officials serving as alternate members on the commission with political allies, according to updates made on the National Capital Planning Commission website.

The president’s arch has faced pushback from historic preservationists and local advocacy groups who argue it will interrupt the visual harmony of the capital, disrupt the peaceful atmosphere at the cemetery and add another obstacle for flights at nearby Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport.

Three Vietnam War veterans sued the Trump administration in February to pause work on the structure, citing concerns over a lack of congressional approval, an obstructed view of Arlington National Cemetery and increased traffic near the construction site.

In another lawsuit filed this month, Arlington County seeks to halt construction pending a thorough environmental review. The complaint alleges the Trump administration did not properly evaluate the project’s potential harm or propose meaningful alternatives as required by federal law. Both lawsuits are ongoing.
entries.author: Kendall Staton

entries.title: Commanders Hire Longtime NFL Coach in an Advisory Role
entries.summary: Steve Wilks, former head coach of the Cardinals, will help with game-planning.
entries.content:
The Commanders have brought in an experienced NFL coach to help Dan Quinn and his staff during the week.

Veteran defensive coordinator Steve Wilks joined the organization last week in a game-planning role. The part-time role will see him assist in practice, but not on gamedays. The news was first reported by NFL Network.

The hire has been in the works since before the season began, according to The Athletic. But Wilks officially joins as Washington is struggling to keep its season on track at 1-4-1. The 57-year-old has bounced between the college and NFL ranks throughout his career and was the head coach of the Arizona Cardinals in 2018. He went 3-13 in his lone season there.

He was also the Panthers’ interim coach in 2022 and went 6-6 in that role. In 2023, he served as the defensive coordinator for a 49ers team that reached the Super Bowl. Last year, he was the Jets’ defensive coordinator, but he was fired in December.

The Commanders are on a bye this week after losing to the 49ers, 23-17, on Monday night. Their next game is Nov. 1 against the Eagles.
entries.author: Alex Schiffer

entries.title: Two Florida Counties Report Federal Agents Outside Early Voting Sites
entries.summary: One election official said they lodged a complaint with the FBI, adding: “to their credit, they are taking this seriously.”
entries.content:
Federal agents have been spotted outside polling locations in two Florida counties this week during early voting, a presence that local election officials say is intimidating and illegal.

Mark Earley, the supervisor of elections in Leon County, said Monday that two Customs and Border Protection vehicles were parked outside the county’s busiest early voting site in Tallahassee for about 10 minutes.

“I have lodged a formal complaint with the FBI, and to their credit, they are taking this seriously,” Earley said in a statement. “Voters should never experience intimidation from anyone when they are voting, and that includes being intimidated by law enforcement or any other governmental officials.”

In Monroe County, masked federal agents were seen conducting an arrest at an intersection near a polling place. Florida’s Local 10 news reported that the location was clearly near an early voting site in Key Largo, with signs that read “Go Vote” and “Vote Here” around the area.

The county’s supervisor of elections, Sherri Hodies, says it violates the law.

“I’m not happy about it. Frankly, I was stunned about it,” Hodie told Local 10 News. “It’s hard to take these phone calls from voters who are frightened. Their voices are shaking.”

Hodie added that she reached out to Customs and Border Protection after the arrest and informed them of all the early voting sites in the county, urging them to conduct business a distance away from those places.

Federal law prohibits federal agents from being present at polling places. But the lead-up to this year’s midterm elections has been rife with concerns from lawmakers and election officials about whether the Trump administration will follow that law or find ways around it.

At Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s confirmation hearing in March, Mullin refused to rule out that agents would stay away from the sites entirely.

“The only reason why my officers would be there is if there was a specific threat for them to be there, not for intimidation,” he said.
entries.author: Adora Brown

entries.title: HHS Was Caught With Erroneous Legal Citations
entries.summary: A filing from the Department of Health and Human Services had "entirely fictitious" citations, and a federal labor agency suggested AI was used.
entries.content:
The Trump administration apparently still hasn’t learned its lesson about double-checking sources.

A federal labor agency flagged so many problems in a recent arbitration filing that it suggested the Department of Health and Human Services used artificial intelligence to draft its brief.

In a section where HHS was arguing that an arbitrator got key facts wrong, one of the government's "supporting legal authorities has a fictitious citation," a Federal Labor Relations Authority decision says.

"The Agency cites 'U.S. Dep’t of the Air Force, 913th Air Wing, 57 FLRA 469, 472 (2001),' which does not exist," the decision says in a footnote.

It was one of 10 "entirely fictitious" citations the agency says it found. And overall, 22 of the HHS filing's 29 footnotes — and 35 of the 42 total legal or record citations — "are fictitious, erroneous, or irrelevant."

This is not the first time HHS has had trouble with citations in the second Trump administration. Last year, The Washington Sun found the department inaccurately cited more than 500 scientific sources to back up its “Make American Healthy Again” commission report — in some cases even making up studies.

In this latest incident, multiple times the decision points out where HHS attorneys cited a case that refers to an irrelevant part of the law. There are also incorrect page numbers, case numbers and other details.

“Based on the nature and scope of these errors, it appears that the Agency may have used a generative artificial-intelligence (AI) tool in drafting its brief,” the decision says.

HHS was asking the FLRA to reverse a decision from a third-party arbitrator who sided with a labor union in a challenge to a presidential memorandum sending federal workers back to in-person work.

HHS not only didn't get what they wanted, but it also got a lecture from FLRA about using AI.

"While nothing prohibits parties from using AI tools when preparing filings for submission to the Authority, we caution those who do so to be aware that AI continues to present significant risks of error," the FLRA wrote.

"Therefore, parties should take steps to verify the accuracy of any AI-generated material and ensure that their filings satisfy all regulatory requirements."

The FLRA used its own footnote there, pointing to a 2024 guidance on the use of AI-based tools in court "on how to follow filing rules when drafting documents using AI, including reviewing and correcting AI-generated text."

The HHS Office of the General Counsel did not respond to a request for comment about whether it used AI to write its filing.

And the issue has popped up elsewhere as AI use has become more widespread. In July, a federal judge cautioned an attorney with the Justice Department about AI use that led to inaccurate citations in an immigration case.

President Donald Trump has embraced artificial intelligence, and multiple agencies across the federal government have confirmed they are using the technology.
entries.author: Ellie Fivas

entries.title: Judge Orders Trump to Sit for Deposition in BBC Defamation Lawsuit by Dec. 11
entries.summary: Trump, who has often avoided depositions, filed his lawsuit against the BBC last December, seeking $10 billion in damages.
entries.content:
By David Fischer and Jocelyn Noveck

MIAMI (AP) — A federal judge on Thursday ordered President Donald Trump to sit for a deposition in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC by Dec. 11.

The order from U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett came as BBC’s lawyers complained that Trump had delayed his appearance. Attorney Charles Tobin said that with two months left in the discovery period, “we still haven’t been able to depose the plaintiff.”

He noted there was an agreed-upon date of Oct. 16, but that the Republican president canceled it for a “matter of national importance.” Tobin said Trump was in fact campaigning in Georgia that day.

“He was participating in party politics and prioritized that over sitting for the deposition,” Tobin said.

Lett said Trump must sit for a deposition by Dec. 11, or face sanctions up to dismissal of his lawsuit — unless the discovery period was extended past Dec. 18.

The BBC asked the judge last week to compel Trump to appear after they said he canceled an agreed-upon date of Oct. 16, citing “matters of national importance.” The British broadcaster says Trump is trying to delay his appearance until January 2027. The judge has threatened sanctions if Trump fails to comply with the court’s schedule.

Trump, who has often avoided depositions, filed his lawsuit against the BBC last December, seeking $10 billion in damages. He accused the publicly funded broadcaster of defamation as well as deceptive and unfair trade practices related to a documentary, “Trump: A Second Chance.”

The BBC acknowledged that filmmakers spliced together quotes from different sections of the speech Trump delivered to his supporters on Jan. 6, 2021, before the storming of the U.S. Capitol, to make it seem he was directly urging violence. The broadcaster apologized over the editing, and the head of the BBC and its top news executive both resigned. But BBC has denied Trump’s claims that it defamed him.

Trump's lawyers say Jack Smith ‘lacks personal knowledge’ of issues in the case


To bolster its defense, the broadcaster subpoenaed former special counsel Jack Smith earlier this month. Trump’s lawyers argued, in a joint filing asking for a hearing on the matter, that there was no good reason for Smith, who is not a party to the case, to appear.

“Smith lacks any personal knowledge regarding the issues in this matter,” they argued in the filing. “He was not present when President Trump’s January 6, 2021, speech … was made, nor did he participate in its preparation. Smith does not have any personal knowledge regarding President Trump’s state of mind at the time the Speech was given.”

Trump's side also argued that “Smith’s testimony would be duplicative,” because he published he lengthy report on the events of January 6 and also testified for many hours. “The entirety of his testimony is publicly available,” it argued.

The BBC countered, in the same filing, that there were few more knowledgeable sources about the events of Jan. 6 than Smith, who studied and investigated them for years.

“It is difficult to imagine a more authoritative source on these issues than Mr. Smith, who spent years gathering evidence on those topics with the force of the Justice Department and the power of the grand jury behind him,” the BBC’s lawyers argued.

“No one forced Plaintiff to file this lawsuit and to dispute that his speech on January 6 incited the violence that followed at the Capitol. But as long as he chooses to maintain the case, he cannot commit the fundamental injustice of preventing the BBC from obtaining the evidence it needs to robustly defend itself on every element of his claim…”

When will Trump sit for a deposition?

In a filing Oct. 13, BBC lawyers said they first requested dates for a deposition in July, and followed up repeatedly, with both sides eventually agreeing on Oct. 16.

After weeks of silence, they wrote, “Plaintiff’s counsel responded on September 28, 2026, indicating that ‘the President is no longer available for his deposition on October 16 due to other matters of national importance’ and that counsel would ‘endeavor to provide you with a replacement date by the end of this week.’ He did not.”

They said they were then told that Trump “has no availability whatsoever for a deposition” before discovery is set to close on Dec. 18, and that Trump would instead make himself available the second or third week of January.

Tobin wrote in the filing. “Those delays have flouted the cooperative spirit of discovery and precluded the BBC from obtaining the evidence necessary to robustly litigate its defense.”
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Ilhan Omar Says She Can’t Continue to Live at Her D.C. Home Post-Raid
entries.summary: The congresswoman said she, her husband and their 20-year-old son were home when federal agents searched their house.
entries.content:
Rep. Ilhan Omar said she is moving out of her Washington, D.C., home after federal agents raided the residence earlier this month.

The Minnesota Democrat, who has faced multiple death threats, told MS Now on Wednesday that she can’t “continue to live there. … So we have to figure out where to move to because our address has been public.”

Omar recounted the raid, which took place on Oct. 12, for the first time in her interview with Chris Hayes. The government said the search was part of an “ongoing federal criminal investigation,” which officials suggested was related to immigration; it has not provided evidence of immigration fraud.

Omar said she was awakened at 6 a.m. to the sound of federal agents banging on her front door. She said she initially thought there was an urgent evacuation happening throughout her neighborhood due to a potential fire.

Omar was at the home with her husband and 20-year-old son, she said.

Her husband answered the door and saw 15 to 25 Homeland Security Investigations agents standing in front of his home, Omar said.

“That’s immigration. That’s trafficking. That’s drugs,” Omar said of the agents assembled. “The fact that they were at my house that early in the morning was so bizarre.”

Omar said agents wanted her to waive her immunity as a member of Congress. She said the agents spent four to five hours going room by room and took 17 items, including several phones, one of which belonged to her youngest daughter. They also took an antique camera that had been gifted to her husband and a Somali-language book for children, she said.

Omar said she asked the agents if they had a search warrant, which they handed over. Omar said that the warrant was specifically for electronics.

“I think ultimately, their goal is to intimidate and scare people from wanting to participate and vote,” she said.

Omar said she takes the Trump administration’s threats to prosecute or denaturalize her “very seriously.” Omar moved to the U.S. from Somalia when she was 12 years old.

“It would be a huge undertaking to, I suppose, indict a 12-year-old for being so cleverly conspiring to defraud immigration services to come to the United States,” she said.
entries.author: Michelle Del Rey

entries.title: 10 Potential Candidates to Replace Mike Locksley at Maryland
entries.summary: After parting ways with the Terps’ football coach, athletic director Jim Smith will lead the search for a replacement.
entries.content:
Mike Locksley’s head coaching tenure at Maryland is over after eight seasons, and the search for his replacement could be a tenure-defining task for athletic director Jim Smith.

Smith has never been part of a major college coaching search. He previously worked for the Atlanta Braves’ business strategy department and was president of the Ohio State Alumni Association. Before that, he worked at Arthur M. Blank Sports and Entertainment, the umbrella company overseeing the Atlanta Falcons and Atlanta United.

Here are some names to keep an eye on as Smith and his staff look for a new football coach.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Dennard Wilson AP - 26025805921657 (3928x2619, AR: 1.50)

Keeping It in the Family


Henry Baker, Temple assistant head coach/interim defensive coordinator: A former defensive back for Maryland in the mid-1990s, Baker has also been an assistant coach for Locksley and helped produce multiple NFL draft picks during his coaching career. Earlier this week, he was named the Owls’ interim defensive coordinator, which will be his first experience calling plays.

Tyler Bowen, Ohio State offensive line coach: Just 37, Bowen played for Randy Edsall and then-offensive coordinator James Franklin at Maryland and later coached with both. He has experience as an offensive coordinator with Virginia Tech and spent a year in the NFL with the Jaguars. Bowen might not be ready for a head coaching role yet, but Smith’s ties to Ohio State could help.

Dennard Wilson, Giants defensive coordinator: The DeMatha graduate has never been a head coach, but he does have experience in both the college and pro game. He also worked in the Bears front office, which is an asset in the world of NIL and the transfer portal. Wilson is just 44 and may have his sights set on bigger jobs, given his career trajectory.

Scott Milanovich, Hamilton Tiger-Cats (CFL) head coach: A former quarterback at Maryland in the ’90s, Milanovich has an interesting resume. He’s never coached in the United States, having held jobs in NFL Europe and the Canadian Football League. But he has been successful, winning three CFL titles. He would face a steep adjustment to American college football, but it could be a risk worth taking.
Charles Huff AP - 26266698435769 (5637x3758, AR: 1.50)

Logical Candidates


Charles Huff, Memphis head coach: Huff might be the candidate. A native of Denton, Maryland, he has won at every program he’s led. He went 32–20 in four seasons at Marshall, improved Southern Miss by six wins in his lone season there and is currently 5–2 in his first season at Memphis. Huff was also Nick Saban’s running backs coach on Alabama’s 2020 national championship team. His track record of showing immediate results should be very attractive to a Terps program that hasn’t generated momentum in years.

Billy Napier, James Madison head coach: The Dukes might be the hottest coaching pipeline in the country. Curt Cignetti led Indiana to the national championship after going 52–9 in five seasons in Harrisonburg. Bob Chesney is off to a hot start at UCLA after leading the Dukes to the College Football Playoff a year ago. Napier turned Louisiana-Lafayette into an FCS powerhouse before struggling to replicate that success at Florida. He’s currently 7–0 at JMU, and may be ready to make the leap to Power 4 football again.

Jake Dickert, Wake Forest: Dickert fits the bill of someone the Terps should target. He’s had success at Washington State and Wake Forest, two places where it can be difficult to win. But Dickert is a Wisconsin native and would be a natural candidate for the Badgers if Luke Fickell gets fired. Does he want to stay east or wait out a chance at going home?

Brian Fleury AP - 26278851055926 (5175x3450, AR: 1.50)

Wild Cards


Biff Poggi, former Charlotte head coach: Poggi is likely not a serious candidate for the job. He went 6–16 in two seasons at Charlotte, but before that he turned St. Frances Academy in Baltimore into a national high school powerhouse. He maintains strong ties to the area, and could be considered for a lesser role on the next coaching staff.

Arthur Smith, former Falcons head coach: Smith has ties to Jim Smith from both the Falcons and Ohio State. He’s also a local, having attended Georgetown Prep where he was an All-Mets selection in football. His NFL experience far outweighs his time in college, and it’s fair to wonder if he’d prefer an NFL job. And his Falcons tenure — three straight 7-10 seasons — wasn’t exactly inspiring.

Brian Fleury, Seahawks offensive coordinator: Fleury’s ties to the state rival Poggi’s and Huff’s. He spent one season at Maryland as a quarterback before transferring to Towson, and he later coached at both. But Fleury had never called plays before this season, and the Seahawks’ title defense is off to a rocky start. He’s an intriguing candidate, but would face a steep learning curve in College Park.
entries.author: Alex Schiffer

entries.title: Afternoon Sun: ‘Hitting Pay Dirt’
entries.content:
Good afternoon. This is the Afternoon Sun newsletter for Oct. 22, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

A federal labor agency accused the Department of Health and Human Services of using AI to draft a document that contained “a fictitious citation.”

  • It wouldn’t be the first time the department ran into trouble with the citations.
Calley Means, a senior adviser to Robert F. Kennedy Jr., resigned from the Trump administration over frustrations that the Make America Healthy Again agenda had stalled, The Wall Street Journal first reported.





THE ADMINISTRATION

Construction on Donald Trump’s arch could start in two weeks if the plans get final approval from a federal commission — one that the president recently stacked with his own appointees.

The State Department ordered some nonessential U.S. diplomatic staff and their family members stationed in Saudi Arabia to depart the region following escalating attacks from Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebel group.

Federal agents were spotted outside polling locations in two Florida counties this week during early voting, a presence that local election officials say is intimidating and illegal.





THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL

Ohio Republican Gov. Mike DeWine denounced a controversial ad featuring the estranged mother of Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton. But Trump enthusiastically defended Acton’s Republican rival, Vivek Ramaswamy, saying on Truth Social that he thought the ad was “so good!”

  • “Who wouldn’t use such an Ad?” Trump wrote. “I would, it’s called, ‘hitting pay dirt.’”




THE HILL

Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minnesota) said she is moving out of her D.C. home after federal agents raided the residence earlier this month.





THE COURTS

Federal authorities charged Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas in a sprawling public corruption case that includes fraud and racketeering accusations involving a cannabis business she co-owns.

Trump will have to sit for a deposition in his $10 billion defamation suit against the BBC by Dec. 11, a federal judge ruled today.

Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio) is asking a federal judge to force the Trump administration to turn over communications about the president’s management of the Kennedy Center, arguing that executive privilege should not shield his decisions as the institution’s chair because the storied performing arts center is not a part of the executive branch.

entries.title: Trump-Linked Crypto Company Accused of ‘Public Corruption’ in New Lawsuit
entries.summary: The lawsuit takes issue with transactions between the Trump-linked cryptocurrency company World Liberty Financial and entities linked to the United Arab Emirates.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump and a cryptocurrency company linked to his family members were sued Thursday over accusations that the president has “corruptly” profited off of more than $2 billion in payments from a foreign government.

The lawsuit, filed by a shareholder for another crypto venture, centers two transactions between World Liberty Financial, a cryptocurrency company founded by Trump and his sons in 2024, and entities linked to the United Arab Emirates. One of the exchanges in question involves a UAE-linked firm’s purchase of close to half of World Liberty Financial’s stake days before Trump assumed office in January 2025.

Trump does not hold direct shares of the crypto company, but the president’s family members indirectly maintain an almost 40% stake in World Liberty Financial.

The plaintiffs argue Trump violated the Constitution’s Foreign Emoluments Clause, which bars federal officeholders from accepting gifts and payments from foreign governments. The suit calls on the court to compel the companies that routed the money to take back any payments made to Trump and order disclosure of any other transactions between foreign parties and the president.

“Using the presidency for personal profit is not only unethical. It is not only a matter of grave concern to millions of Americans,” the lawsuit says. “It is illegal, and it is a clear violation of the Constitution President Trump swore to protect.”

David Wachsman, a spokesperson for World Liberty Financial, told The Washington Sun that the claims in the lawsuit “are without merit, and we look forward to resolving them in court."

“World Liberty Financial is compliant with all U.S. laws and regulations,” Wachsman said. “No one at World Liberty Financial works for the U.S. Government.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Spokesperson Anna Kelly told Politico that “there are no conflicts of interest” and called the lawsuit “frivolous.”

Trump’s June disclosure of more than $1.1 billion in crypto earnings prompted backlash from lawmakers across the aisle this year, including legislation to regulate politicians’ power to trade crypto. Senate Democrats ultimately blocked the House-passed measure in September over the lack of specific ethics provisions that would rein in Trump’s crypto interests.

J. Benjamin Greenberg, who holds shares in the Circle Internet Group crypto company, filed the lawsuit in D.C. district court on Thursday and is also seeking “compensatory and punitive damages.”

Both Circle and World Liberty issue dollar-pledged stablecoins, and Greenberg’s suit asserts that the Trump family’s deals with the UAE firms gave World Liberty Financial’s stablecoin a “competitive advantage that Circle cannot match.”

Trump sold his 49% direct stake in the company to a UAE-backed investment firm, and his son Eric Trump signed off on the transaction on Jan. 16, 2025.

“Millions of dollars from that deal, routed from a foreign government, flowed to President Trump after he assumed office,” Karianne Jones, an attorney for Greenberg, wrote in the complaint.

The legal challenge also references a separate UAE-linked investment company’s purchase of $2 billion in World Liberty Financial stablecoin in May 2025.

“Weeks after President Trump took office, an investment fund created by the UAE government orchestrated a scheme to inflate the value of President Trump’s crypto holdings by purchasing $2 billion in the President’s brand-new digital currency,” Jones wrote. “The corrupt purchase handed President Trump millions of dollars in interest and dramatically expanded the circulation of his stablecoin overnight.”

Greenberg, who holds 10,000 shares of Circle’s Class A common stock, filed the lawsuit on behalf of the crypto company, but a Circle spokesperson appeared to distance the business from the legal complaint in a statement shared with The Washington Sun

“This lawsuit was filed by an individual shareholder, not by Circle,” the spokesperson said. “Circle did not initiate, direct, authorize, or participate in the filing. We do not comment on pending litigation.”

entries.title: ICE Extends Contract for Company After Delayed Detainee Medical Payments
entries.summary: The agency says Acentra Health is the only company up to the task.
entries.content:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement extended this week a contract worth up to $982 million with the company hired to process medical claims for detainees.

Acentra Health this month launched the processing services for health providers caring for people in immigration detention, nearly a year after ICE originally contracted the company to pay out the claims, according to the company’s website.

During the lapse in claims processing the agency has racked up millions owed to ambulance services, hospitals and other providers. Detainees have received bills for medical care, the San Francisco Chronicle reported.

And Democratic lawmakers have raised concerns that the lack of payment for off-site medical claims led to an increase in detainee deaths and health complications. Acentra Health has said government shutdowns caused the delay.

The Virginia-based company could get paid the sum to process the claims until Oct. 24, 2030, according to a federal contracting database.

So far, ICE has committed to paying the company nearly $134 million, according to the contracting database. ICE extended the work with Acentra Health on Tuesday, increasing the potential award amount, according to a government notice.

“Any lapse in the current medical claims management and provider payment support would create immediate and significant risks to [ICE Health Service Corps] operations and to the health and safety of the detained population,” a document ICE published Tuesday says. “Maintaining support through Acentra mitigates these risks because the contractor is already performing the required services.”

ICE rushed in October 2025 to find a contractor after the Department of Veterans Affairs abruptly ended the two decade-long agreement to handle the claims. The health care technology company has also processed medical claims for the VA since 2017, according to an FAQ page about the contract with ICE.

The agency originally awarded the contract to Acentra Health without any competition because it was urgent to hire a company to pay out the claims to ensure immigrants got timely critical medical care, according to a document from the agency.

Acentra Health remains the only contractor that can provide support immediately after the agency tried to identify other potential vendors in June, ICE stated in its justification for extending the contract on Tuesday. But the company repeatedly pushed back the date for when it would start processing the claims, first expected to begin by April 30.

Lindsey Rodarmer, Acentra Health’s public relations manager, told The Washington Sun in July that the Department of Homeland Security shutdown had delayed implementation of the system. The company was required to pause its work until it received an extension in June, according to its FAQ on the contract issue.

“Acentra Health began implementation work at its own financial risk in late October 2025, before receiving payment for that work,” the company website says. “This work included establishing technical environments, setting up data services and software configurations, and recruiting and training staff to support the letter contract.”

entries.title: Trump Enthusiastically Endorses Ramaswamy’s Controversial Attack Ad
entries.summary: “It’s so good!” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump enthusiastically endorsed a controversial attack ad produced by Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign, which featured his Democratic opponent’s estranged mother calling her a liar.

Lawmakers and political personalities on both sides of the aisle have come out against the spot because of the way it uses the family history of Amy Acton, who is running against Ramaswamy.

Acton has accused her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, of sexually abusing her as a child, and he was arrested on rape charges in the 1970s. Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, subsequently lost custody of her but stayed with her husband for years after the accusations.

Trump didn’t see a problem with the use of Acton’s mother as a character witness against her daughter, writing in a Truth Social post that he thought the ad was “so good!”

“Who wouldn’t use such an Ad?” Trump continued. “I would, it’s called, ‘hitting pay dirt.’”

The president accused the press of conspiring in a “concerted and well-coordinated attack” in an attempt to get Ramaswamy to back away from the ad, which has been denounced by lawmakers on both sides of the aisle.

On Thursday, Ohio Republican Gov. Mike DeWine called the ad “deeply, deeply troubling” and urged Ramaswamy’s campaign to take it down.

“It’s wrong to run this ad,” he said.

Trump called those remarks “disloyal to the Republican Party” and suggested Ramaswamy continue running the commercial so voters can “listen to the mother of a defective, dishonest, and incapable Candidate, explain how the daughter is a DISASTER who, uncontrollably, lies, cheats, and steals!”

He also referred to Acton as “Lyin’ Amy Acton.”

In the ad, Donna Arthur says her daughter “has a serious problem” before telling Ohioans not to vote for her. “She is a liar. She lies about her past.”

The president commended Acton’s mother for coming forward.

“That took a lot of courage to do but, essentially, what she was really doing was saving Ohio from making a truly horrible choice!” he wrote.

Acton’s campaign released an ad Tuesday in which her brother, Phil Stearns, recounted their alleged childhood abuse, saying Acton “got the worst of it.”

The Acton commercial’s on-screen text says: “Amy suffered physical and sexual abuse by her stepfather for years. She and Phil have been estranged from their mother ever since.”

Trump isn’t the only high-profile Republican who has endorsed Ramaswamy’s ad. On Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance told Republicans to “stop whining” about the commercial as he spoke in Ohio.

“I have to admit that I’m a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America,” he said.
