entries.title: Trayon White’s Lawyer Says the Government Is Targeting Him Based on Race
entries.summary: Federal prosecutors announced Thursday they will seek a second trial and a new indictment against White, the D.C. Council member accused of bribery.
entries.content:
Prosecutors intend to seek a new indictment and proceed with a new trial against D.C. Council member Trayon White, they announced in court Thursday — a proposal met with strong opposition from White’s defense attorneys, who said the lawmaker was being unfairly targeted in part because of his race.

In a hearing in U.S. District Court, Assistant U.S. Attorney Rebecca Ross said she expected a new trial could begin in May at the absolute earliest. Ross said the government intends to seek a superseding indictment from a grand jury, which would replace the original indictment against White and could contain different or new charges.

White, 42, faced trial for bribery last month and stands accused of accepting cash as part of a corrupt agreement to influence city contracts. But the proceeding ended in a mistrial when the jury could not agree on a verdict; nine jurors wanted to acquit White and three wanted to convict him, according to White’s attorneys. On the day the judge declared the mistrial, U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro’s office swiftly released a public statement saying it would retry the case — but Ross’s statements Thursday entered the plan into the official court record.

The announcement means the embattled lawmaker, who represents Ward 8 on the council, is in for a lengthy extension of his more than two-year legal saga. His defense attorney Gary Kohlman said the government’s decision appeared calculated “to put [White] in a situation where he will be defenseless,” given how expensive it would be for White to retain his current lawyers. Kohlman also said that if the council member was white, prosecutors would “never consider” re-trying the case after a jury split 9-3 in favor of acquittal.

“In over 50 years of practice. I've never made that accusation before, never, not once,” Kohlman told reporters afterward, referring to his statements about racial bias. “Trayon White is African American. He represents, by and large, an African American community that has repeatedly elected him. He had nine people out of 12 that found him not guilty in this case, and I cannot think of any other explanation.”

Asked about Kohlman’s statements at an unrelated news conference Thursday, Pirro called the claim of racial bias “absurd.”

“We don’t care what color he is,” she said. “We care about the people of this District.”

White was arrested in August 2024 and accused of accepting $35,000 — and agreeing to accept upwards of $150,000 — in illegal bribes. The charges stemmed from meetings White had with a businessman named Allieu Kamara in the summer of 2024. Unbeknownst to White at the time, the FBI was recording their conversations because Kamara, who faced separate criminal charges of his own, agreed to act as a confidential informant to help them investigate the council member.

The videos show White accepting envelopes of cash and the two men discussing business. In the tapes, Kamara, a prolific D.C. government contractor, repeatedly asked White for help securing lucrative government grants for violence-interruption work. White agreed, and the two men discussed plans to further Kamara’s business with the city, including in other areas such as mental health services.

But White’s attorneys argued that the lawmaker never took serious steps to carry out the alleged bribery scheme and said the cash payments, which they acknowledged White accepted, could have been political donations. D.C. officials testified in court that White had discussed Kamara’s businesses with them but had never pressured them to extend the grants.

To convict White of bribery, 12 jurors would have to have agreed that White actually intended to carry out the agreement to influence the contracts. For nine, Kohlman said, the government’s evidence did not clear the bar.

Now, the prospect of a new trial and many months of additional litigation in the interim may mean White has to get new lawyers. In the FBI recordings shown at trial, White could be heard telling Kamara that he was “bankrupt”; other evidence the government agreed not to introduce to the jury showed that White also struggled with gambling debts. Kohlman said continuing with his current legal team may be prohibitively expensive.

“This is designed to break the back of Mr. White’s efforts to effectively defend himself,” Kohlman said.

Pirro said her office’s responsibility is to follow the law and pursue justice.

“We don’t throw up our hands in the air and say, ‘Oh, we’re going to go home, let it go,’” she said. “No — he took the cash. Let a jury decide.”

White declined to comment on the prospect of another indictment and trial, saying he stood by the statements of his attorney. Asked by a television reporter what the money was for, if it wasn’t a bribe, White was silent.

entries.title: Veterans Ask Judge to Block Construction of Trump’s Triumphal Arch
entries.summary: The request follows a Trump administration court filing that said construction for the arch could start as soon as Nov. 5.
entries.content:
A group of veterans asked a federal judge for a preliminary injunction to halt construction of President Donald Trump’s triumphal arch, which the administration says could begin as soon as Nov. 5.

The Thursday filing argues that building the 250-foot arch is “unauthorized by any law” since Congress has not passed a statute allowing its construction. It requests a ruling on the motion no later than Nov. 4, the day before the Trump administration said in a filing Wednesday it could begin construction.

The request is the latest move in a lawsuit filed by three Vietnam War veterans in February over the construction of the arch.

The veterans argue that erecting the arch — between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery — would permanently interfere with and degrade the “symbolic landscape that holds great personal meaning” to the plaintiffs.

The veterans regularly visit the cemetery to pay their respects and admire “the solemnity of the reciprocal views between the Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial,” the filing says.

The request for preliminary injunction comes after the Wednesday court filing said that construction could “commence immediately” if the National Capital Planning Commission, a panel that approves projects on federal land in the D.C. area, approves the plan in a Nov. 5 meeting and the Interior Department authorizes work.

entries.title: Supreme Court Rules New Hampshire Can Limit Student ID Use for Voting
entries.summary: Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the sole dissenter on the unsigned order.
entries.content:
The Supreme Court on Thursday cleared the way for New Hampshire to implement its ban on voters using student IDs to prove their identity when obtaining a ballot.

The one-page order, unsigned and accompanied by a two-page dissent from Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, ended a monthslong legal fight over how the state informs voters about the change in election law.

The ruling pointed to the Purcell principle, which advises against altering voting guidance on the eve of an election.

“The District Court did not point to anything that would justify deviating from that principle,” the order says.

New Hampshire’s ban on using student IDs went into effect in June, but state officials went to the Supreme Court after a federal judge ruled that the state must update its guidance about the law to local election officials.

On Oct. 2, the federal judge ruled that while student IDs are not valid to establish voter identity, the state needed to clarify that local election officials may consider the documents, “along with other available evidence, when determining voter identity.”

State officials told the Supreme Court on Oct. 15 that the change would be “a complete reversal of prior guidance and training,” and inconsistent with documents used by election officials for reference on Election Day.

“If the injunction is not stayed, there is a substantial risk of inconsistent application of identity-verification procedures,” the state officials told the Supreme Court.

And the misunderstanding could mean “there is substantial risk that voters could show up at the polls with only their student IDs in-hand,” the state officials said.

Attorneys for the Coalition for Open Democracy, a voting rights group, had told the Supreme Court that the ruling didn't change the law, just the guidance that was reissued quickly after the Oct. 2 ruling.

The secretary of state’s website said prior to the Supreme Court ruling that “even though student identification cards are not expressly valid to prove voter identity, pursuant to court order they may be considered along with other available evidence when determining if a voter has proven their identity when registering to vote.”

“His website has told voters since the October 2 Order that supervisors may consider a student ID along with other evidence," the voters' filing says. "The Secretary’s revised guidance is now the status quo. A stay wouldn’t preserve it. It would reverse the rules for a second time in a month.”

In her dissent, Jackson says the Purcell principle does not seem to apply in this case, saying the lower court made a “targeted order, requiring only that the relevant government official conform his public statements to the letter of state law.” The district court’s injunction was meant to “address alleged misinformation, not to change the law,” she added.

“I respectfully dissent because — even, and perhaps especially, when an election is looming — I would not disturb a clearly justifiable federal-court order issued to ensure that the public receives accurate information about a State’s electoral processes,” Jackson wrote.

entries.title: Ruptured Gas Line Prompts Power Outages Around Metro Center
entries.summary: A construction project at the Hotel Harrington caused the gas leak, leading to power outages and street closures.
entries.content:
Buildings around Penn Quarter lost power Thursday evening after a gas line ruptured during construction at the Hotel Harrington, according to the D.C. Fire and EMS Department.

Fire Department officials said in a social media post that, because of the rupture's severity, crews had to shut off power at the hotel at 436 11th St. NW, which affected surrounding blocks. The post added that Pepco was working to restore power.

Pepco told The Washington Sun in a statement around 6:30 p.m. that it had fully restored power after temporarily shutting it off at the hotel and surrounding blocks for “the safety of the public and first responders.”

Earlier in the evening, Pepco’s website had said 12 active outages in the area surrounding the hotel were affecting 39 customers, with outages expected to be restored from 7 p.m. to 11 p.m.

D.C. Fire shut down several roads after the gas leak. Officials closed the 400 and 500 blocks of 11th Street Northwest, between F Street and Pennsylvania Avenue; the 1100 block of E Street Northwest, between 11th and 12th streets; and the 1100 block of F Street Northwest, between 11th Street and 12th Street.

The D.C. Council posted on social media that electricity had been cut to several buildings, including the Wilson Building, which houses the council, and that traffic in the area was also disrupted.

The Hotel Harrington, which opened in 1914, was the District’s longest-running hotel until its closure three years ago. A California private equity firm bought the hotel in July for $14.4 million and has been renovating the property, the Washington Business Journal reported.

D.C. Fire did not respond to requests for comment.

This story has been updated to include a statement from Pepco.

entries.title: DOJ Investigating Corey Lewandowski Over Alleged Contract Misconduct At DHS: Reports
entries.summary: Lewandowski’s lawyer denied that any investigation is taking place.
entries.content:
The Justice Department is looking into allegations of contract misconduct connected to Corey Lewandowski, who served as a top adviser for former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, after the department received a criminal referral from the DHS Inspector General’s office.

The office has been examining accusations of Lewandowski’s mishandling of contracts during Noem’s tenure leading the department, The Wall Street Journal first reported Thursday — though Lewandowski’s lawyer denied that any investigation exists at all.

“Mr. Lewandowski has not been contacted by the Justice Department regarding any investigation, and he denies any wrongdoing when he was proudly serving his country in a voluntary capacity,” Adam Trigg, Lewandowski’s attorney, wrote in a statement to The Washington Sun.

President Donald Trump fired Noem in March as the secretary faced a slew of controversies, including the department’s handling of immigration enforcement efforts in Minnesota, a $220 million border security ad campaign and the purchase and contract procurement for several aircraft.

Asked about the investigation into Lewandowski, the White House pointed to Trump’s comments to reporters on Thursday: “I want my people to be honest, and if they're not going to be honest, they have to be prosecuted. I don’t know about specifically, but I view it as if people are not honest, they're stealing from me as President.”

Lewandowski expects a pardon from Trump in the event he is charged in a criminal case, the Journal reported Thursday. Trump appeared to pour cold water on that idea.

“If somebody is dishonest, I consider them not only against the country; I consider that dishonest against me. So I will never do anything to stop a prosecution if someone is dishonest,” Trump said.

DHS did not immediately return a request for comment for this story.

News of the investigation comes days after The Sun first reported that the purchases of several aircraft at the end of Noem’s tenure were tied to an “ongoing criminal law enforcement investigation,” citing a letter from DHS’ Privacy Office.

The acknowledgement was part of a denial of an Oct. 14 Freedom of Information Act request filed by The Sun, which sought information about the purchases of the planes. The Sun is appealing the denial.

In a statement after the publication of The Sun’s story, a DHS spokesperson claimed the FOIA response had been sent to The Sun in “error.” The DHS FOIA office did not return a request for comment.

The New York Times previously reported that several of the planes were bought above market value from Daedalus Aviation Corporation, whose chair donated $10,000 to a pro-Noem super PAC.

In March, House Democrats on the Oversight and Homeland Security committees called on DHS’s watchdog office to investigate Lewandowski.

A White House spokesperson on Tuesday deferred to DHS when asked about the criminal inquiry. A DOJ spokesperson initially declined to comment on the matter, but on Tuesday told The Sun it does not comment on the existence of ongoing investigations.
